Finite geometry

Combinatorics OurBigBook.com
Finite geometry studies geometric incidence structures having finitely many points, such as finite projective and affine spaces.

Increasing subsequence

Words: 38 Articles: 1
Combinatorics OurBigBook.com
An increasing subsequence of a sequence x1​,…,xn​ is a sequence xi1​​≤⋯≤xim​​ selected at indices i1​<⋯<im​.

Longest increasing subsequence (L(x))

Words: 21
Increasing subsequence OurBigBook.com
A longest increasing subsequence is an increasing subsequence of maximum length. Changing or deleting one term changes its length by at most one.

Additive combinatorics

Words: 3k Articles: 83
Combinatorics OurBigBook.com
Additive combinatorics studies how the sizes and representation functions of sumsets reveal algebraic structure in subsets of abelian groups.

Sum-product phenomenon

Words: 53 Articles: 1
Additive combinatorics OurBigBook.com
The sum-product phenomenon says that a finite subset of a field cannot usually have both a small sumset and a small product set unless it has additional subfield-like structure.

Solymosi sum-product theorem over the complex numbers

Words: 26
Sum-product phenomenon OurBigBook.com
For finite U,V,W⊆C with U={0} and W={0},
∣U+V∣∣UW∣≥561​∣U∣3/2∣V∣1/2∣W∣1/2.
(1)
In particular, addition and multiplication cannot both expand a nontrivial finite set of complex numbers only slightly.

Density of a finite subset (δ(A)=∣A∣/∣X∣)

Words: 16
Additive combinatorics OurBigBook.com
The density of A in a nonempty finite ambient set X is the proportion ∣A∣/∣X∣.

Sidon set

Words: 39
Additive combinatorics OurBigBook.com
A Sidon set in an abelian group is a subset A for which an equality a+b=c+d with a,b,c,d∈A forces the unordered pairs {a,b} and {c,d} to be equal. Equivalently, the ordered nonzero differences a−b with a=b are all distinct.

Linear configuration count

Words: 75 Articles: 1
Additive combinatorics OurBigBook.com
A linear configuration count is a weighted sum over tuples satisfying prescribed linear equations. Orthogonality of complex exponentials often rewrites such a count as an integral of Fourier transforms.

Fourier stability of a linear configuration count

Words: 48
Linear configuration count OurBigBook.com
Suppose a linear configuration count has a Fourier-integral representation with k factors. If one has a uniform Fourier bound for the difference between two weights and compatible Lk−1 bounds for each weight, expanding the difference one factor at a time and applying Hölder's inequality bounds the change in the count.

Transference principle in additive combinatorics

Words: 255 Articles: 4
Additive combinatorics OurBigBook.com
A transference principle replaces a function bounded by a sparse pseudorandom majorant with a bounded dense model that is indistinguishable by a chosen family of tests. Results for bounded functions can then be transferred to the sparse setting.

Test-function seminorm (∥⋅∥F​)

Words: 91 Articles: 1
Transference principle in additive combinatorics OurBigBook.com
For a family F of real-valued functions on a finite set and normalized inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩, the test-function seminorm is
∥g∥F​=supf∈F​∣⟨g,f⟩∣.
(2)
It measures the largest correlation of g with an allowed test. It is a seminorm, and becomes a norm when the tests separate points.
Dual test-function norm (∥⋅∥F∗​)
Words: 44
Test-function seminorm OurBigBook.com
The dual test-function norm is
∥g∥F∗​=sup∥h∥F​≤1​∣⟨g,h⟩∣.
(3)
If F is closed, convex, and symmetric, the Bipolar theorem for a dual pair identifies its dual unit ball with F. Submultiplicativity under pointwise products allows a polynomial in one test function to remain controlled in this norm.

Dense model theorem for a multiplicative test family

Words: 126 Articles: 1
Transference principle in additive combinatorics OurBigBook.com
Let F be a closed, convex, symmetric family of functions into [−1,1] that contains the constant function 1, and suppose its dual test-function norm is submultiplicative under pointwise products. If a nonnegative majorant ν has average at most one and ∥ν−1∥F​ is exponentially small in 1/ε, then every 0≤g≤ν has a dense model 0≤g​≤1 satisfying
∥g−g​∥F​≤ε.
(4)
The proof separates g from the convex set of dense models, then approximates the positive part of the separating test by a polynomial. Submultiplicativity controls every power in that polynomial.
Polynomial approximation of the positive part
Words: 35
Dense model theorem for a multiplicative test family OurBigBook.com
On any fixed compact interval, the positive part of a real-valued function t+​=max(0,t) can be approximated uniformly by a real polynomial. Quantitative dense-model arguments use a version whose degree and coefficient growth are explicitly controlled in terms of the approximation error.

Sumset (A+B)

Words: 48 Articles: 1
Additive combinatorics OurBigBook.com
For subsets A,B of an additive group, their sumset is A+B={a+b:a∈A,b∈B}.

Iterated sumset (mA)

Words: 34
Sumset OurBigBook.com
For a nonnegative integer m, the iterated sumset mA is the sum of m copies of A, with 0A={0}. Repetitions are allowed, so its elements are sums a1​+⋯+am​ with each ai​∈A.

Difference set (A−B)

Words: 15
Additive combinatorics OurBigBook.com
For subsets A,B of an additive group, their difference set is A−B={a−b:a∈A,b∈B}.

Doubling constant (∣A+A∣/∣A∣)

Words: 339 Articles: 10
Additive combinatorics OurBigBook.com
The doubling constant of a nonempty finite set A is ∣A+A∣/∣A∣. A small doubling constant indicates that A behaves approximately like a coset of a subgroup.

Words: 181 Articles: 5
Doubling constant OurBigBook.com
If finite sets satisfy ∣A+B∣≤K∣A∣, then the Plünnecke-Ruzsa inequality bounds iterated sumsets and difference sets by
∣ℓB−mB∣≤Kℓ+m∣A∣.
(5)
Petridis minimal-growth lemma
Words: 36
Plünnecke-Ruzsa inequality OurBigBook.com
If a nonempty finite set X minimizes ∣X+B∣/∣X∣ among the nonempty subsets of A, with minimum K′, then
∣X+B+C∣≤K′∣X+C∣
(6)
for every finite set C. Iteration is a short proof of the Plünnecke-Ruzsa inequality.
Ruzsa triangle inequality
Words: 124 Articles: 3
Plünnecke-Ruzsa inequality OurBigBook.com
For finite subsets A,B,C of an abelian group with A nonempty,
∣B−C∣≤∣A∣∣A+B∣∣A+C∣​.
(7)
An injective encoding chooses one representation of each element of B−C and translates it by every element of A.
Noncommutative Ruzsa triangle inequality
Words: 92 Articles: 2
Ruzsa triangle inequality OurBigBook.com
For nonempty finite subsets A,B,C of an arbitrary group,
∣A∣∣BC−1∣≤∣AB−1∣∣AC−1∣.
(8)
Choose one representation x=bx​cx−1​ for each x∈BC−1. The map (a,x)↦(abx−1​,acx−1​) is injective.

Words: 21
Noncommutative Ruzsa triangle inequality OurBigBook.com
If a finite subset A of a group satisfies ∣A3∣≤K∣A∣, then repeated use of the Noncommutative Ruzsa triangle inequality gives
∣A4∣≤K3∣A∣≤K4∣A∣.
(9)
Small doubling does not control tripling in a noncommutative group
Words: 47
Noncommutative Ruzsa triangle inequality OurBigBook.com
Let H be a finite subgroup and choose x with H∩xHx−1={1}. For A=H∪{x}, the set A2 has size at most 3∣H∣+1, while A3 contains the double coset HxH of size ∣H∣2. Thus bounded doubling alone gives no tripling bound in arbitrary groups.

Doubling constant OurBigBook.com
For every K, a finite set A in an abelian group with ∣A+A∣≤K∣A∣ is contained in a coset progression of rank and relative size bounded in terms of K alone.

Words: 17
Freiman-Ruzsa theorem OurBigBook.com
If A⊆Fpn​ and ∣A+A∣≤K∣A∣, then A is contained in a vector subspace H satisfying
∣H∣≤K2pK4∣A∣.
(10)
Szemerédi theorem in a bounded-rank coset progression
Words: 48
Freiman-Ruzsa theorem OurBigBook.com
For fixed density δ>0, rank r, and progression length, every sufficiently large proper coset progression of rank at most r has the property that each subset of relative density at least δ contains a nontrivial arithmetic progression of that length. This follows from the multidimensional Szemerédi theorem.
Small difference set forces a three-term arithmetic progression
Words: 35
Freiman-Ruzsa theorem OurBigBook.com
For every C there is N(C) such that a set A⊆Z with ∣A∣≥N(C) and ∣A−A∣≤C∣A∣ contains a nontrivial three-term arithmetic progression. The Freiman-Ruzsa theorem places A densely in a bounded-rank coset progression, where the Szemerédi theorem in a bounded-rank coset progression applies.

Approximate group

Words: 382 Articles: 8
Additive combinatorics OurBigBook.com
A K-approximate group is a finite symmetric subset of a group A for which some set X with ∣X∣≤K satisfies A2⊆XA. In additive notation the covering condition is A+A⊆X+A.

Intersection of an approximate group power with a subgroup

Words: 54
Approximate group OurBigBook.com

A finite point set is cyclic transitive when a cyclic group of isometries acts transitively on it.
Kriz theorem for cyclic transitive point sets
Words: 66 Articles: 1
Cyclic transitive point set OurBigBook.com
Every finite cyclic transitive point set is a Euclidean Ramsey set. In particular every regular polygon is Euclidean Ramsey.
A-invariant coloring of a Cartesian power (A-invariant coloring of a Cartesian power)
Words: 55
Kriz theorem for cyclic transitive point sets OurBigBook.com
For A⊆X, a coloring of Xn is A-invariant when changing any coordinates from one member of A to another does not change the color. A product argument upgrades the existence of a copy of X on which A is monochromatic to an A-invariant copy of every finite Cartesian power Xn.

Symmetric function

Words: 124 Articles: 5
Combinatorics OurBigBook.com
A symmetric function is a formal power series of bounded total degree that is invariant under every finite permutation of its variables. Symmetric functions form a graded ring with several useful bases.

Complete homogeneous symmetric polynomial (hn​)

Words: 23
Symmetric function OurBigBook.com
The complete homogeneous symmetric polynomial hn​ is the sum of all monomials of total degree n. Its generating function is
H(t)=∑n≥0​hn​tn=exp(∑k≥1​kpk​tk​).
(122)

The Schur polynomials form a basis of the ring of symmetric functions indexed by integer partitions.

Jacobi–Trudi identity

Words: 13

The Jacobi–Trudi identity expresses a Schur polynomial as
sλ​=det(hλi​−i+j​).
(123)
In particular, s(a,b)​=ha​hb​−ha+1​hb−1​.
